## What we would carry back into the room {#carry .stop data-stop="carry"}

::: {.year}
The end of it
:::

::: {.lead}
What we came away with, loosely ordered by how much weight we would put on each. Not
instructions — a record of what the reading suggested.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Everything cited on the previous pages, weighed as part three weighs it. Nothing new is
introduced here.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="context"}
The figure from part four, repeated because it is the thing to leave with. Everything
physical about the touch stays where it is; only what it is taken to mean changes.
:::

::: {.rules}
- **Slower than feels natural — about a hand's width a second.**\
  One to ten centimetres a second is where the research clusters, and it is slower than
  most of us work by default.
- **Warmth seems to matter about as much as speed.**\
  Around skin temperature — hands, oil, room. Cold shifted every speed toward less
  pleasant, and technique did not appear to make up for it.
- **Hairy skin looks like the home ground, though not the only ground.**\
  Forearm, back, shoulders. The palm has some of these fibres after all — just fewer.
- **Still contact seems to count.**\
  Resting a hand is not a lesser version of stroking. It may be preferred to stroking
  done wrong.
- **What you are trying to do decides which system you are working with.**\
  Fine detail comes through a fingertip on hairless skin. Contact and comfort come
  through a broad, slow, warm hand on hairy skin.
- **Averages describe populations, not the person on the table.**\
  The curve is an average across a lot of people. We would ask, watch and adjust rather
  than put a number on someone.
- **Saying what you are about to do matters more than we expected.**\
  You have access the social map normally saves for the people we are closest to. Saying
  it out loud seems to be how that stays safe rather than just allowed.
- **Describing the touch travels further than describing the mechanism.**\
  "Slow, warm, light, moving" is honest and checkable. "Activating your C-tactile fibres"
  goes beyond the evidence.
- **The hormone claims are the ones we would hold most loosely.**\
  That evidence is the thinnest thing here. The pain and comfort findings are steadier
  and need no help from it.
- **Most of the work is probably not being done by the fibres.**\
  Safety, consent, predictability and relationship. The fibres are the doorway, not the
  visit.
:::

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
If someone leaves your room with one thing, we would want it to be the touch rather than
the mechanism: slow, warm, unhurried, and from someone they agreed to be touched by.
That is the part with the most behind it, and it is the part they will remember.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Everything cited above, and two entries that are not cited anywhere: Morrison (2010) and
Suvilehto (2023) are in the list because they are worth reading, not because a claim on
these pages rests on them.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="revisions"}
Four corrections the field has made to its own published work, kept in view on the way
out. A literature that revises itself in the open is the reason the rest of this list is
worth anything.
:::

Where to go next, in the order we would send someone.

::: {.reading}
[McGlone et al. (2014)](https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S0896-6273(14)00387-0){.n}
— The standard overview, free to read, and the source most people are quoting
second-hand. Long, but the first half is very approachable.

[Morrison et al. (2010)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00221-009-2007-y){.n}
— The friendliest conceptual framing of why any of this might matter.

[Kidd et al. (2023)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17437199.2021.1980082){.n}
— The bridge from nerve fibres to stress physiology, and the closest thing to a review
written for people who do this for a living.

[Suvilehto et al. (2023)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44159-023-00217-5){.n}
— The widest recent view — who touches whom, where, and what for.
:::

::: {.foot}
Assembled in 2026 from the literature as it stood. A reading of published
research, written for people who work with touch. It is not medical advice, it does not
describe a technique, and it cannot tell you what the person in front of you wants. Where
researchers disagree we have tried to say so rather than tidy it away — that is not
hedging, it is the current state of a young field still arguing productively with
itself.
:::

::: {.refnote}
The list below is numbered in the order the journey met each source, so it reads as a

:::
